title: T-Cell Exhaustion in Mathematical Models of Oncolytic Immunovirotherapy: A Structured Review
content: Oncolytic immunovirotherapy combines direct tumour-cell lysis with immune activation, but clinical responses remain variable and durable survival benefit is not consistently observed. T-cell exhaustion, the progressive loss of effector function under sustained antigenic stimulation, has been proposed as one explanation for this discrepancy. Whether the existing modelling literature is able to express that explanation has not been examined systematically. This review assembles the published mechanistic models of oncolytic virotherapy and of T-cell exhaustion and classifies them along six structural criteria: the tumour compartments represented, the treatment of free virus, the form of the immune response, whether exhaustion is dynamic, whether the model was calibrated, and whether it was validated. Twenty-nine models are compared; a further fourteen records met the inclusion criteria but could not be accessed and are listed in Appendix A. Each pairwise combination of tumour, replicating virus and dynamic exhaustion is represented in the literature, but no retrieved model contains all three: models that include a virus treat immune efficacy as a parameter, while models in which exhaustion evolves over time contain no virus or, in one case, no tumour. The obstacle appears to be disciplinary rather than mathematical, since a reduced exhaustion formulation adds a single state variable to an existing tumour–virus–immune model. Calibration is weak across both literatures, and no retrieved study fits a model to longitudinal exhaustion markers alongside viral load, so a combined model would currently be formulable but not identifiable. We therefore set out the structural requirements for such a model and the measurements that would be needed to constrain it.
